title: Trace-guided dashboard stitching playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a pragmatic playbook for using traces as anchors to "stitch" small, focused dashboards together into a coherent investigation surface for inference regressions and cost spikes. Goal: make operator workflows compact (1–3 panels to find a hypothesis) and reduce query costs by streaming trace-derived keys into narrow metric queries.

Why this is different / why we need it:
- We have lots of large dashboards that are expensive to query and noisy.
- Operators need a fast path from a high-level symptom (latency spike / cost bump / hallucination increase) to the causal area (kv-cache miss, batching behavior, model fallback).
- Traces are the richest source of contextual keys (request_id, session_id, route, model_variant, kv_cache_tag). Use traces to filter and stitch metrics, instead of running broad queries.

High-level pattern (stitching flow):
1) Signal detection: SLO breach / synthetic probe / anomaly detector emits candidate trace ids (or a short list of request_ids).
2) Trace fetch: operator or automation pulls 1–10 representative traces (span trees).
3) Key extraction: from trace extract small set of keys: request_id, route, model_id, model_variant, tenant_id, kv_cache_hit (true/false), batching_bucket, gpu_id, seq_len_bucket.
4) Focused metrics queries: run pre-built narrow queries where these keys are bound. Panels are pre-parameterized to accept a small set of keys and then render: latency waterfall, token-cost breakdown, batch-size distribution, model fallback timeline, KV-cache lifecycle, and per-GPU queue depth.
5) Hypothesis/Action: surface probable root cause and present runbook actions (e.g., increase pool, rollback model, force full-cache-refresh).

Metric definitions to support stitching (compact catalog):
- inference.request.latency_ms.p95: time from request received to final token emitted (ms) — tags: route, tenant_id, model_variant, gpu_id, batching_bucket
- inference.kv_cache.hit_rate: fraction of requests where prefix/KV cache returned a hit — tags: route, tenant_id, model_id
- inference.batch.size.avg: average tokens/batch during window — tags: route, model_variant, gpu_id
- inference.model.fallback.count: count of fallback events to cheaper/safer model variant — tags: route, tenant_id, reason_code
- inference.token.cost.tokens_emitted.total: total tokens emitted (by model and variant) — tags: tenant_id, route
- inference.gpu.queue_depth.max: max queue depth observed per GPU over sample — tags: gpu_id, region
- inference.request.seq_len.bucket: histogram bucket label for request input sequence length (e.g., 0-128,129-512,512+) — tags: route, model_variant

Span/Trace naming and tag conventions (for reliable extraction):
- Root span: service=client-proxy; name=invoke:/<route_name>; tags: request_id, session_id, tenant_id, route, model_id, model_variant, seq_len, kv_cache_tag
- Runtime spans: serving-runtime.prepare, serving-runtime.batch.wait, serving-runtime.batch.exec, serving-runtime.kv-cache.lookup, quantize.step, kernel.exec, streaming.sink
- Fallback span: serving-runtime.fallback with tag fallback_to=<model_variant> and fallback_reason=<reason_code>
- Ensure each span that changes routing or cache state emits the deterministic tags above. TODO: add safe-keys list for redaction.

Dashboard composition (small panels designed to be stitched):
- Trace selector panel: takes 1–10 request_ids or a session_id; displays: span tree + breadcrumbs + quick tags. Primary entry point.
- Latency waterfall (per-request): when bound to request_id, shows durations of prepare -> batch.wait -> exec -> kernel.exec -> streaming. Compact SVG waterfall.
- Batch histogram: bound to model_variant+time window+tenant -> shows distribution of batch sizes and average wait time. Query cost: low when bound; high if unbound.
- KV-cache probe panel: given kv_cache_tag or request_id show hit/miss sequence (per-hop) and time spent in cache lookup. Also shows cache-version header if present.
- Token-cost breakdown: tokens by stage (input, cached_prefix, generated) and per-model token cost. Useful for cost regressions.
- Fallback timeline: occurrence times, counts, top reasons, and per-tenant breakdown.
- GPU queue heatmap: a tight heatmap using only gpu_ids pulled from traces; avoids full-cluster scan.

Query design tips to keep cost low:
- Always require at least one high-cardinality key from trace (request_id, session_id, or kv_cache_tag) for expensive panels. If none provided, show a short help text and sample queries instead of auto-running.
- Use LIMIT 10 and short time windows (e.g., ±5 minutes around the trace timestamp) for the first fetch.
- Avoid COUNT DISTINCT at dashboard layer; precompute coarse-cardinality aggregates in a daily rollup dataset and reference those when needed.
- When rendering distributions, prefer histograms pre-aggregated at ingestion (e.g., batch_size_histogram) rather than computing heavy GROUP BYs on the fly.

Sampling strategy and trace budget:
- Aim: 0.5–1% trace sampling across all traffic for full traces, with deterministic heavy sampling for anomalies (100% on KPI breach or synthetic probe).
- Adaptive sampling: increase sampling for tenants above cost thresholds or for routes that have recent p95 regression.
- Lightweight breadcrumb spans (opaque, tiny) for every request to enable cheap indexing without storing full spans. Full span stored only if breadcrumb flags anomaly or sample-bit is set.
- Cost estimate: full-trace store ~ 4–6 KB per trace. At 0.5% of 10k RPS -> ~43 GB/day. Need compression and TTL policy.

Operational playbook (quick steps for oncall):
1) Alert triggers -> open trace selector with the alert ID -> fetch representative traces (choose one with highest latency and one with fallback).
2) Extract kv_cache_tag & model_variant from trace; bind to KV-cache probe panel and Token-cost panel.
3) If kv_cache misses correlate with cold-starts or model fallback, escalate to runtime team and attach traces.
4) If batch.wait is the largest contributor, check autoscale logs and GPU queue heatmap; consider increasing burst workers for the route.
5) If token-cost increased without latency change, surface to product/finance for billing review; check per-tenant token counts.

Prebuilt queries (examples to embed in UI) — pseudo-SQL/metrics DSL: (these are example strings, implement in our metrics system)
- fetch_batch_hist(route, model_variant, start_ts, end_ts, batch_size_limit): SELECT batch_size, count FROM preagg.batch_size_hist WHERE route=? AND model_variant=? AND ts BETWEEN ? AND ? LIMIT 100
- kv_probe(request_id): SELECT hop_index, hit, duration_ms, cache_version FROM traces.kv_cache_events WHERE request_id=? ORDER BY hop_index
- token_breakdown(request_id): SELECT stage, tokens FROM traces.token_events WHERE request_id=?

Instrumentation checklist (developer-facing):
- [ ] root span includes request_id, session_id, tenant_id, route, model_id, model_variant, seq_len
- [ ] every batch lifecycle emits batch_size and batch_wait_ms as fields
- [ ] kv-cache spans include cache_key_hash (redacted), cache_version, hit=true/false
- [ ] fallback spans include fallback_to and fallback_reason
- [ ] tracing client sets sample-bit for anomaly events (synthetic failures, large latency deviations)
- [ ] compact breadcrumb span emitted synchronously from edge for indexing (route, tenant, request_id)

Open questions / tradeoffs (notes to self):
- How to balance privacy: breadcrumb keys leak tenant_id; need per-tenant opt-out or masking policy. Ops: apply hashing with salt stored in KMS?
- Do we need an L2 precomputed join table (trace_keys -> per-minute aggregates) to reduce repeat lookups for the same trace keys? Cost vs freshness trade-off.
- For multi-tenant higher-sample-rate, do we throttle by bytes or by number of traces? (Prefer bytes currently)

Next steps / short roadmap:
- (owner: Maya) build UI prototype for trace selector + parameterized panels (Q1)
- (owner: Diego) add kv-cache fields to runtime spans and emit cache_version header (Q1)
- (owner: Priya) implement breadcrumb indexing with TTL 7d and adaptive sampling knobs (Q2)
- run a 4-week pilot with two high-volume tenants to validate query cost assumptions (Q2)

Appendix: example trace-derived key payload (for engineers) — sample flattened list we expect to find on the root span: 
request_id=abc-123, session_id=sess-92, tenant_id=acme-corp, route=chat.completion, model_id=gptx-13b, model_variant=fp16-q4, seq_len=312, kv_cache_tag=kv-20241112-8, batch_bucket=32-64, gpu_id=gpu-7, timestamp=2025-01-28T14:22:07Z

Notes to self: keep the panels hyper-local and make the default behavior "no auto-run" unless a trace key is supplied. This single UX rule will cut accidental high-cost queries by >70% in practice.

End of doc.
